ta-l1d3q1-d1e99.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 3, where Lombard shows the unity of essence by natural reasons and the Trinity of persons by likenesses in creatures (vestige, then image). Thomas organizes Lombard's four proofs of God's unity under Dionysius's three ways of ascending from creatures to God. Because the creature has its being from another, we are led either to the cause of what is received (causality) or, given the imperfect mode of reception, to remove imperfection from God (remotion) and to place in him the received perfection more nobly (eminence). The four arguments run as follows. (1) Causality: whatever is from nothing is from another, ultimately from one first. (2) Remotion: beyond bodies, which are finite and mobile, and beyond mutable incorporeal beings, there must be something incorporeal, immutable, and wholly perfect. (3) Eminence in being: good and better imply a best. (4) Eminence in knowledge: degrees of beauty (speciositas) imply a principle of beauty. Thomas then maps the treatment of the vestige and the image and announces two inquiries, on the knowledge of God and on the vestige, the first in four articles: God's knowability, whether his existence is self-evident, whether he is known through creatures and by whom, and what the philosophers could know of him.
claims: There are three ways from creatures to God: causality, remotion, and eminence.
These three ways follow from the creature's having its being from another and receiving it imperfectly.
Lombard's four proofs of God's unity correspond to causality, remotion, eminence in being, and eminence in knowledge.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e142.summary: First objection that God is not knowable by a created intellect. Dionysius says we can neither speak of nor understand God, since knowledge concerns existing things and God is above all existing things.
claims: Knowledge is only of existing things, and God is above all that exists.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e145.summary: Second objection. God is further from any intelligible known to us than the intelligible is from the sensible, and sense cannot know the intelligible. So our intellect cannot know God.
claims: The distance between God and creaturely intelligibles exceeds that between intelligible and sensible.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e148.summary: Third objection. All knowledge is through a species that assimilates knower to known, and no species can be abstracted from God, since he is supremely simple.
claims: All knowledge is through a species, and none can be abstracted from God.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e152.summary: Fourth objection. The infinite as such is unknown (the Philosopher), because something of it always lies outside the one grasping it, and God is infinite.
claims: Every infinite is unknown because it exceeds what grasps it.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e155.summary: Fifth objection. Phantasms are to the intellect as colours are to sight, so our intellect understands nothing without a phantasm. No phantasm can be formed of God ('To what image will you liken him?', Isa. 40:18), so he is not knowable by our intellect.
claims: Our intellect understands nothing without a phantasm, and none can be formed of God.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e161.summary: Sed contra from Jeremiah 9:24: let whoever glories glory in knowing me. God would not exhort to vainglory, so knowing God is possible.
claims: Scripture exhorts us to glory in knowing God.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e167.summary: Second sed contra. Even according to the Philosopher, contemplating God is the ultimate end of human life. If humans could not reach it they would have been made in vain, since what fails to attain its end is vain (cf. Ps. 88:48).
claims: Contemplation of God is the ultimate end of human life, and a nature ordered to an unattainable end would be vain.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e172.summary: Third sed contra. The intelligible differs from the sensible because an excessive sensible destroys sense, whereas the highest intelligible strengthens the intellect. God is supremely intelligible in himself as the first intelligible, so his excellence is no obstacle and our intellect can understand him.
claims: An excellent intelligible strengthens rather than destroys the intellect.
God, as first intelligible, is maximally knowable in himself.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e175.summary: Thomas's determination. The question is not whether God can be seen immediately in his essence, which is treated elsewhere, but whether he can be known in any way. God is knowable, but not so as to be comprehended. Every knower knows according to its own mode, not the mode of the thing known, and no creature's mode reaches the height of the divine majesty. So no one knows God perfectly as he knows himself.
claims: God is knowable but not comprehensible by any creature.
Every knower knows according to its own mode, and no created mode reaches God's majesty.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e179.summary: Reply to the first objection. God does not exist as other existents do, but the nature of being is in him eminently. Since he is not wholly without being, he is not wholly without knowability, though he is not known in the way of other existents that a created intellect can comprehend.
claims: God possesses being eminently and so is not wholly unknowable, though not comprehended like other existents.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e182.summary: Reply to the second objection. In the property of his nature God is further from any intelligible than the intelligible is from the sensible, but in the character of knowability he agrees more with it. Whatever is separate from matter is knowable as intelligible, while what is material is known as sensible.
claims: What is separate from matter has the character of an intelligible; God thus agrees with intelligibles in knowability.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e185.summary: Reply to the third objection. The species by which a thing is known exists in the knowing power according to the knower's mode. Of things more material than the intellect, the species is simpler in the intellect than in the things, which is why they are known by abstraction. God and the angels are simpler than our intellect, and the species of them produced in it is less simple. They are known not by abstraction but by their impression on our intellect.
claims: Species exist in the knower according to the knower's mode.
God and angels are known not by abstraction but by impression on our intellect.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e188.summary: Reply to the fourth objection, distinguishing two kinds of infinity. The privatively infinite naturally ought to have a limit and lacks one; it is imperfect and known only in a qualified way. The negatively infinite is in no way limited; it is most perfect and extends to all things, and so cannot be comprehended by a created intellect but only attained.
claims: God is negatively, not privatively, infinite and can be attained but not comprehended.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e191.summary: Reply to the fifth objection. The Philosopher is speaking of the intellectual knowledge connatural to us in this life, in which God is known only through phantasms, not of himself but of his effects, through which we reach him. This does not rule out a higher, non-natural knowledge through the influence of divine light, for which no phantasm is needed.
claims: In this life God is known naturally through phantasms of his effects.
A higher knowledge through divine light does not require phantasms.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e194.summary: Concedes the remaining sed contra arguments.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e198.summary: Qualifies the last sed contra, which would imply that God is now supremely known by us. Intellect and sense are alike in that neither can reach what is not proportioned to it, since all knowledge is according to the knower's mode (Boethius). They are unlike in that an excessive intelligible does not corrupt the intellect. The intellect fails to know the supreme intelligible not because it is corrupted but because it does not reach it, so a created intellect cannot see God perfectly.
claims: The intellect fails to know God perfectly not through corruption but through lack of proportion.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e210.summary: First objection that God's existence is self-evident. Self-evident things are those whose knowledge is naturally implanted in us, and according to Damascene the knowledge that God exists is naturally implanted in all.
claims: Damascene holds that knowledge of God's existence is naturally implanted in all.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e213.summary: Second objection. Intellectual light is to the intellect as sensible light is to sight. Visible light is seen through itself, and nothing is seen except through it, so God is known immediately through himself.
claims: Intellectual light is known through itself as visible light is seen through itself.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e216.summary: Third objection. All knowledge is through union of the known with the knower, and God is intrinsic to the soul through himself, more than the soul is to itself. So he can be known through himself.
claims: God is more intimately present to the soul than the soul to itself.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e220.summary: Fourth objection. What cannot be thought not to exist is self-evident, and God cannot be thought not to exist. This is proved by Anselm's argument: God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, and what cannot be thought not to exist is greater than what can. It is also proved from Avicenna: nothing can be thought without its quiddity, and God's quiddity is his very being.
claims: God, as that than which nothing greater can be thought, cannot be thought not to exist.
God's quiddity is his being, so he cannot be thought without existing.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e223.summary: Sed contra. Self-evident things, though they may be denied in speech, can never be denied in the heart (the Philosopher). But 'the fool said in his heart, there is no God' (Ps. 13:1), so God's existence is not self-evident.
claims: What is self-evident cannot be inwardly denied, but God's existence can be.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e229.summary: Second sed contra. What is concluded by demonstration is not self-evident, and the philosophers demonstrate that God exists.
claims: God's existence is demonstrated and therefore not self-evident.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e232.summary: Thomas's determination. A thing's knowability can be considered in itself or with respect to us. In himself, God's existence is self-evident and he is understood through himself, not made intelligible by us as material things are. With respect to us there are two cases. As regards his likeness and participation, his being is self-evident, since nothing is known except through its truth, which is modeled on God, and that truth exists is self-evident. As regards the supposit, God as he is in his incorporeal nature, it is not self-evident. Many have denied it, such as Democritus and others who posited no agent cause. What is self-evident to us is known at once from sense, as with whole and part, whereas from sensibles we reach God only by reasoning that they are caused, that every effect has an agent cause, and that the first agent is not a body. This is Avicenna's argument.
claims: God's existence is self-evident in itself but not to us as regards his nature.
As regards his participated likeness (truth), God's being is self-evident to us.
We reach God's existence only by reasoning from sensible effects.
concepts: per se notum secundum se vs. quoad nos

ta-l1d3q1-d1e238.summary: Reply to the first objection. Damascene speaks of a knowledge of God implanted in us according to his likeness, not according to his own nature. In the same way all things desire God not as he is in his nature but in his likeness, since nothing is desired, or known, except insofar as it bears his likeness.
claims: The innate knowledge of God concerns his likeness, not his nature.
All things desire and know God only in his likeness.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e241.summary: Reply to the second objection. Sight is proportioned to see bodily light through itself, but our intellect is proportioned to know naturally only through sensibles. It can reach pure intelligibles only by reasoning.
claims: Our intellect reaches pure intelligibles only by reasoning from sensibles.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e245.summary: Reply to the third objection. God is in the soul by essence, presence, and power, but not as an object of the intellect, which knowledge requires. The soul too is present to itself, yet knowing the soul is very difficult and is reached only by reasoning from objects to acts and from acts to powers.
claims: God's presence in the soul is not presence as an object of intellect.
The soul knows itself only by reasoning from objects to acts and from acts to powers.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e248.summary: Reply to the fourth objection on Anselm. Once we understand what God is, we cannot understand him to be God and also able to be thought not to exist. But it does not follow that someone cannot deny or think that God does not exist, since one can think that nothing exists than which a greater cannot be thought. Anselm's argument proceeds on the supposition that such a thing exists.
claims: Anselm's argument works only on the supposition that something than which nothing greater can be thought exists.
One can coherently think that no such being exists.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e251.summary: Applies the same reply to the Avicennian proof from the identity of God's quiddity and being.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e264.summary: First argument that humans can know God through creatures. Romans 1:20 says the invisible things of God are seen, being understood through the things that are made 'by the creature of the world', which, on Lombard's exposition, is the human being.
claims: Romans 1:20 teaches that humans know God's invisible things through created things.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e270.summary: Argues that angels know God through creatures. Such knowledge consists in seeing divine goodness shining in creatures, and an angel knowing things in their own kind sees divine goodness in them.
claims: Angels see divine goodness shining in creatures.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e273.summary: Argues that brutes know God. Only someone who knows a command can receive one, and in Jonah 4 the Lord commanded a worm to strike the ivy, so the worm knew the command and the commander.
claims: God commanded a worm in Jonah 4.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e277.summary: Argues that sinners know God, from Romans 1:21: when they knew God they did not glorify him as God.
claims: Romans 1:21 attributes knowledge of God to sinners.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e283.summary: Contrary argument. Every effect that leads to knowledge of its cause is somehow proportioned to it, and creatures are not proportioned to God. So humans cannot come to know him from them.
claims: An effect leads to knowledge of its cause only if somehow proportioned to it.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e286.summary: Argues that angels do not know God through creatures. What is known through itself is not known through another, and angels know God through himself, seeing him in his essence.
claims: Angels see God in his essence.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e289.summary: Argues that brutes cannot know God. A power fixed in an organ can know only material species, since knowledge follows the knower's mode. Brutes have only sensitive, organic cognitive powers, so they cannot know the wholly immaterial God.
claims: Organic powers can know only material species.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e292.summary: Argues that sinners cannot know God. Ambrose comments on 'Blessed are the pure of heart, for they shall see God' (Matt. 5:8) that others will not see him, since the wicked will not see God.
claims: Only the pure of heart will see God.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e298.summary: Thomas's determination. Creatures proceed from God exemplarily, as from a cause that is somehow similar by analogy, each imitating him as far as its nature allows. So one can ascend from creatures to God by causality, remotion, and eminence. This requires two things. First, the knower must be able to grasp God in some way, which excludes brutes. Second, the knowledge must begin from creatures and end in the Creator, which excludes angels and the blessed, who proceed from knowledge of the Creator to creatures. The process therefore belongs to humans in this life, good and bad alike.
claims: Creatures lead to God by analogy, through causality, remotion, and eminence.
Knowing God through creatures belongs to wayfaring humans, good and bad, but not to brutes, angels, or the blessed.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e302.summary: Concedes the first argument (from Rom. 1:20) that humans know God through creatures.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e305.summary: Reply to the second argument. An angel knows divine goodness shining in creatures, but it does not come from the creature to the Creator; it goes the other way.
claims: Angels know creatures from God, not God from creatures.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e308.summary: Reply to the third argument. God's command did not reach the worm so that it grasped the command's intent. By divine power its natural estimative faculty was moved to carry out what God was arranging.
claims: Brutes execute divine commands through their natural estimative power moved by God, not by grasping them.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e311.summary: Concedes the fourth argument, that sinners can know God.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e314.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. The creature is an effect not proportioned to the Creator, so it leads not to perfect knowledge of him but to imperfect knowledge.
claims: Creatures, as disproportioned effects, yield only imperfect knowledge of God.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e317.summary: Concedes the sixth and seventh arguments, that angels and brutes do not know God through creatures.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e321.summary: Reply to the eighth argument. Ambrose speaks of the vision of God through his essence in heaven, which no wicked person will attain; likewise only the faithful attain the knowledge of faith. But natural knowledge of God is common to good and bad, faithful and unfaithful.
claims: Natural knowledge of God is common to good and wicked; vision and faith are not.
concepts: natural vs. faith vs. glory knowledge

ta-l1d3q1-d1e333.summary: First argument that the philosophers reached the Trinity by natural knowledge. Aristotle says we magnify the one God by the number three, and Plato and others speak of a paternal intellect.
claims: Aristotle and Plato appear to speak of a triadic God and a paternal intellect.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e342.summary: Second argument. The philosophers could know what shines forth in creatures, and the soul bears an express likeness of the Trinity. Through their study of the soul's powers they could have reached the Trinity.
claims: The soul bears an express likeness of the Trinity.
concepts: image of the Trinity in the soul

ta-l1d3q1-d1e345.summary: Third argument from Richard of St Victor: for the explanation of any necessary truth, not only probable but necessary arguments are available. Knowing the Trinity is necessary, so the philosophers could have had reasons for it, as the proofs in Distinction 2, art. 4 suggest.
claims: Richard of St Victor holds that necessary arguments exist for every necessary truth.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e352.summary: Fourth argument. The Gloss on Romans 1 says the philosophers did not reach knowledge of the third person, and on Exodus 8 that Pharaoh's magicians failed at the third sign. So the philosophers seem at least to have known two persons.
claims: The Gloss implies philosophers knew two divine persons but not the Holy Spirit.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e355.summary: Sed contra from Hebrews 11:1: faith is the argument of things not apparent. That God is three and one is an article of faith and so is not evident to reason.
claims: The Trinity, as an article of faith, is not evident to reason.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e361.summary: Thomas's determination. Natural reason cannot reach knowledge of the Trinity, so the philosophers knew nothing of it except perhaps through revelation or hearsay. Natural reason knows God only from creatures, and everything said of God with respect to creatures pertains to the essence, not the persons. So natural reason reaches only the essential attributes. The philosophers could, however, know the persons through what is appropriated to them, in knowing power, wisdom, and goodness.
claims: Natural reason cannot know the Trinity of persons.
Everything known of God from creatures pertains to the essence, not the persons.
Philosophers could know the persons only through appropriated attributes.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e364.summary: Reply to the first argument. According to the Commentator, Aristotle did not mean to posit a Trinity of persons. Because perfection appears in triads in all creatures (beginning, middle, end), the ancients honoured God with threefold sacrifices and prayers. Plato is said to have learned much about divine things from Old Testament books found in Egypt, or by 'paternal intellect' he may mean the divine intellect conceiving the idea of the world, the archetypal world.
claims: Aristotle's ternary refers to the perfection of triads in creatures, not to the Trinity.
Plato's paternal intellect may be the divine intellect containing the archetypal world.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e367.summary: Reply to the second argument. The likeness of the Trinity in the soul is wholly imperfect and deficient, as Lombard will say. It is called 'express' only in comparison with the likeness of a vestige.
claims: The image of the Trinity in the soul is imperfect and is 'express' only relative to the vestige.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e370.summary: Reply to the third argument. Taken universally, Richard's claim that every truth can be proved by reason is plainly false, since self-evident first principles are not proved. Things known in themselves but hidden to us are proved through what is better known to us, namely effects. The Trinity cannot be proved from creaturely effects, so it cannot be proved at all, and the reasons given are fitting adaptations rather than necessary conclusions. If, per impossibile, the distinction of persons were removed, God would still have supreme goodness, beatitude, and charity.
claims: Not every truth can be proved; first principles are not demonstrated.
The Trinity cannot be proved from effects, and arguments for it are only arguments of fittingness.
Supreme goodness, beatitude, and charity would remain in God even abstracting from the persons.

ta-l1d3q1-d1e374.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The philosophers did not know two persons as to their proper features but only as to what is appropriated to them. They knew these not as appropriated, which would depend on knowing the proper features, but as attributes of the divine nature. Why then not goodness, appropriated to the Spirit? They did not know goodness in its chief effect, the incarnation and redemption, or they did not venerate and imitate divine goodness as they venerated power and wisdom.
claims: Philosophers knew appropriated attributes as essential attributes, not as appropriated to persons.
They lacked knowledge of divine goodness in its chief effect, incarnation and redemption.

ta-l1d3q1-Dd1e94.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 3 maps Lombard's proofs of the divine unity from natural reason and of the Trinity from creaturely likenesses (vestige and image). It arranges his four arguments under Dionysius's three ways of causality, remotion, and eminence, grounded in the creature's having being from another and receiving it imperfectly. It announces the questions on the knowledge of God and on the vestige.
claims: The three ways from creatures to God follow from the creature's derived and imperfect being.

ta-l1d3q1-Dd1e134.summary: Article 1 asks whether God is knowable by a created intellect. Objections invoke Dionysius's claim that God is beyond being and knowledge, the disproportion of God to our intellect, the impossibility of abstracting a species from God, the unknowability of the infinite, and the need for phantasms. Thomas holds that God is knowable but not comprehensible, since each knower knows according to its own mode. The replies explain that God has being eminently and is intelligible by immateriality, and that he is known by impression, not abstraction. He is negatively, not privatively, infinite and can be attained but not comprehended. Natural knowledge in this life goes through phantasms of his effects, but divine light permits higher knowledge, and the intellect falls short of God through disproportion, not corruption.
claims: God is knowable by creatures but comprehensible by none.
God is negatively infinite, attainable but not comprehensible.

ta-l1d3q1-Dd1e202.summary: Article 2 asks whether God's existence is self-evident. Objections appeal to Damascene's innate knowledge, to the analogy of light, to God's intimate presence in the soul, and to Anselm's and Avicenna's arguments. Against them stand the fool's denial and the existence of demonstrations. Thomas distinguishes the self-evident in itself from the self-evident to us. God's existence is self-evident in itself. To us it is self-evident only with respect to his participated likeness, since that truth exists is self-evident, and not with respect to his nature, which we reach only by reasoning from sensible effects. Anselm's argument holds only on the supposition that a greatest conceivable being exists.
claims: God's existence is self-evident in itself but not to us; we reach it by demonstration from effects.
Anselm's argument presupposes the existence of that than which nothing greater can be thought.

ta-l1d3q1-Dd1e256.summary: Article 3 asks whether God can be known through creatures, and by whom. Thomas holds that because creatures proceed exemplarily from God as from an analogically similar cause, one can reach God from them by causality, remotion, and eminence. This requires the capacity to grasp God and a cognition that begins from creatures. It therefore belongs to humans in this life, good and bad alike, and not to brutes, angels, or the blessed. Creatures, as disproportioned effects, yield only imperfect knowledge. Brutes execute divine commands through estimative instinct, and natural knowledge is common to the wicked, while faith and vision are not.
claims: Wayfaring humans, good and bad, can know God through creatures by analogy; brutes, angels, and the blessed do not.
Knowledge of God through creatures is imperfect.

ta-l1d3q1-Dd1e325.summary: Article 4 asks whether the philosophers could reach the Trinity from creatures. Objections cite Aristotle's ternary, Plato's paternal intellect, the image in the soul, Richard of St Victor's necessary reasons, and the Gloss's claim that they knew two persons. Thomas holds that natural reason, which knows God only from creatures, reaches only the essential attributes, never the persons, except through appropriated attributes known as essential. The replies reinterpret Aristotle and Plato and call the soul's image imperfect. They deny that every truth can be proved, treating arguments for the Trinity as arguments of fittingness. And they explain the philosophers' ignorance of divine goodness through their ignorance of the incarnation and redemption.
claims: The Trinity cannot be known or proved by natural reason; arguments for it are arguments of fittingness.
Philosophers could know the persons only through appropriated essential attributes.

ta-l1d3q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 3 treats the knowledge of God attainable through creatures, the epistemological counterpart of Lombard's natural proofs of divine unity. The Prooemium arranges those proofs under the three Dionysian ways of causality, remotion, and eminence. Article 1 holds that God is knowable by creatures but never comprehended, since every knower knows according to its own mode and God is negatively infinite. Article 2 holds that God's existence is self-evident in itself but not to us, except as regards his participated likeness in truth. We reach it by demonstration from effects, and Anselm's argument holds only on a supposition. Article 3 assigns knowledge of God through creatures, grounded in analogical exemplarity, to wayfaring humans, good and bad, and not to brutes, angels, or the blessed. Article 4 denies that natural reason can reach the Trinity. It attains only the essential attributes, and the Trinitarian arguments are arguments of fittingness, not demonstrations.
claims: God is knowable but incomprehensible to every creature.
God's existence is self-evident in itself but demonstrated to us from effects.
Wayfaring humans know God through creatures by causality, remotion, and eminence.
Natural reason cannot reach the Trinity of persons.
